source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: IV lorazepam is prescribed. Which item in the client's history should make the nurse consult the prescriber first?
questions.rationale: Lorazepam is contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma, coma, existing CNS depression, uncontrolled severe pain, and pregnancy or breastfeeding.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1429 (PDF p. 1738)
questions.quote: contraindicated in clients who are comatose, with preexisting central nervous system (CNS) depression, with uncontrolled severe pain, and those with narrow-angle glaucoma.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which baseline laboratory tests does the nurse expect before a client starts risperidone?
questions.rationale: Baseline renal and liver function tests are done before risperidone, which is used cautiously in renal or hepatic impairment.
explanations: Lithium levels are for lithium therapy.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1431 (PDF p. 1740)
questions.quote: Baseline assessment includes renal and liver function tests

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Quinidine gluconate is prescribed. Which condition in the record is a CONTRAINDICATION?
questions.rationale: Quinidine is contraindicated in complete AV block, intraventricular conduction defects, escape rhythms, and myasthenia gravis. It is used with caution in asthma.
explanations: Not a contraindication unless it is myasthenia gravis.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1462 (PDF p. 1771)
questions.quote: It is contraindicated in complete AV block, intraventricular conduction defects

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client has received tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). Which item should the nurse keep at hand as part of standard care?
questions.rationale: tPA dissolves clots, and bleeding is a frequent adverse effect. The nurse tests urine, stool, and NG drainage for occult blood.
explanations: Useful, but not specific to the risk.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1468 (PDF p. 1777)
questions.quote: Equipment needed by the nurse would include occult blood test strips to monitor for occult blood

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse monitor for MOST often in a client on hydrochlorothiazide?
questions.rationale: Thiazides are potassium-losing. Other effects include hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, and hyperglycemia.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1472 (PDF p. 1781)
questions.quote: The client taking a potassium-losing diuretic must be monitored for decreased potassium levels.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: The nurse has just given a dose of diazepam. What is MOST important before leaving the room?
options: Place a bedpan within easy reach
Tell the client to call for help
questions.rationale: Diazepam commonly causes dizziness, drowsiness, and lethargy, so the nurse puts safety measures in place: side rails up and assistance when getting out of bed.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1473 (PDF p. 1782)
questions.quote: The most frequent side effects of this medication are dizziness, drowsiness, and lethargy.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease takes benztropine daily. Which side effect should the nurse specifically monitor for?
questions.rationale: Benztropine is anticholinergic and can cause urinary retention, so intake and output are monitored. The nurse watches for dysuria, distention, small voidings, and overflow incontinence.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1476 (PDF p. 1785)
questions.quote: Urinary retention is a side effect of benztropine mesylate, an anticholinergic medication.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with AIDS and CMV retinitis is on ganciclovir. Which nursing action is appropriate?
options: Give it only on an empty stomach
Use bleeding precautions such as a soft toothbrush
questions.rationale: Ganciclovir frequently causes neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, so the nurse uses bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, electric razor) and watches for bleeding.
explanations: Not a key effect of ganciclovir.
Correct: thrombocytopenia raises the bleeding risk.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1478 (PDF p. 1787)
questions.quote: Ganciclovir causes neutropenia and thrombocytopenia as the most frequent side effects.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on quinidine for ventricular ectopy develops diarrhea and nausea. What should the client do?
options: Stop the drug until it passes
Halve the dose on their own
Notify the provider but keep taking it
questions.rationale: GI upset and dizziness are common with quinidine and are reported, but the client never stops the drug. A sudden fall in the drug level can trigger dysrhythmias.
explanations: The dose is never changed by the client.
Correct: report it, but keep taking the drug.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1479 (PDF p. 1788)
questions.quote: A rapid decrease in the medication level of an antidysrhythmic could precipitate dysrhythmia.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus asks what vasopressin will do. The nurse explains that it:
questions.rationale: Vasopressin, an antidiuretic, increases water reabsorption in the renal tubules and decreases urine output. It also causes vasoconstriction and stimulates peristalsis and smooth muscle.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1481 (PDF p. 1790)
questions.quote: increases reabsorption of water by the renal tubules, resulting in decreased urinary output.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client well controlled on glyburide now has fasting glucose of 180 to 200 mg/dL. Which drug on the record may be the cause?
questions.rationale: Corticosteroids, thiazides, and lithium can reduce glyburide's effect and cause hyperglycemia. The other drugs may enhance its effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1482 (PDF p. 1791)
questions.quote: Corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics, and lithium may decrease the effect of glyburide, causing hyperglycemia.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which statement about buspirone should the nurse include in client teaching?
options: It carries a high risk of addiction
questions.rationale: Buspirone's side effects (dizziness, nausea, headache, lightheadedness) are usually minor. Unlike benzodiazepines, it is not addicting, tolerance does not develop, and it is not strongly sedating.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1483 (PDF p. 1792)
questions.quote: Dizziness, nausea, headaches, lightheadedness, and paradoxical central nervous system excitement, which generally are not major problems, are side effects of the medication.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client taking cyclosporine after a kidney transplant should be MOST alert for:
questions.rationale: Immunosuppression increases the risk of infection, so the client reports signs of infection. Other effects include hypertension, hirsutism, tremors, and gingival hyperplasia.
explanations: Correct: immunosuppression raises the infection risk.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1484 (PDF p. 1793)
questions.quote: The client should be especially alert for signs and symptoms of infection while taking this medication

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client with Tourette's syndrome receives haloperidol decanoate. How does this drug act?
options: It blocks dopamine receptors in the brain
questions.rationale: Haloperidol decanoate is a long-acting antipsychotic that blocks dopamine at postsynaptic receptors. Fluoxetine blocks serotonin reuptake, donepezil inhibits acetylcholine breakdown, and imipramine blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1490 (PDF p. 1799)
questions.quote: acts by blocking the binding of dopamine to the postsynaptic dopamine receptors in the brain.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client to mix regular and NPH insulin in one syringe. Which instruction is correct?
options: Draw up the NPH insulin first
Roll the NPH bottle between the palms
questions.rationale: The NPH bottle is rotated between the hands to resuspend the insulin; shaking causes bubbles that alter the dose. Regular insulin is drawn up first. Bottles in use may be kept at room temperature.
explanations: Regular is drawn up before NPH.
Shaking causes foaming and dosing errors.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1491 (PDF p. 1800)
questions.quote: The NPH insulin bottle needs to be rotated for at least 1 minute between both hands.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which common side effect should the nurse watch for after giving preoperative scopolamine?
questions.rationale: Scopolamine is anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, decreased sweating, and dilated pupils. The distractors are the opposites of these effects.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1495 (PDF p. 1804)
questions.quote: Scopolamine is an anticholinergic medication that causes the frequent side effects of dry mouth, urinary retention, decreased sweating, and dilation of the pupils.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: When should a client take a single daily dose of imipramine?
questions.rationale: Imipramine causes fatigue and drowsiness, so a single daily dose is taken at bedtime. Alcohol is avoided, and effects may take at least 2 weeks to appear.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1496 (PDF p. 1805)
questions.quote: The client should be instructed to take the medication (a single dose) at bedtime and not in the morning because it causes fatigue and drowsiness.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Metoclopramide four times daily is prescribed for diabetic gastroparesis. When should the nurse schedule it?
options: With each meal and at bedtime
30 minutes before meals and at bedtime
One hour after meals and at bedtime
questions.rationale: Metoclopramide stimulates upper GI motility. Giving it 30 minutes before meals lets it start working before food arrives.
explanations: Too late to prepare the GI tract.
Correct: before meals and at bedtime.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1501 (PDF p. 1810)
questions.quote: The client should be taught to take this medication 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client is to take magnesium citrate after barium GI studies. How should it be taken?
options: With a tepid glass of water
Chilled, with a full glass of water
questions.rationale: Magnesium citrate solution is served chilled with a full glass of water and should not stand for long, which flattens the carbonation and makes it less palatable.
explanations: Correct: chilled, with a full glass of water.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1504 (PDF p. 1813)
questions.quote: It should be served chilled and taken with a full glass of water.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with chronic pancreatitis starts pancrelipase. Which effect should the nurse tell the client to expect?
questions.rationale: Pancrelipase is a digestive enzyme that reduces steatorrhea and improves nutrition. It does not treat pain or heartburn and does not regulate glucose.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1505 (PDF p. 1814)
questions.quote: The medication should reduce the amount of fatty stools (steatorrhea).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A postoperative client complains of gas pains. Which prescribed drug should the nurse look for?
questions.rationale: Simethicone is an antiflatulent that relieves pain from excess GI gas. Droperidol treats nausea, and magnesium hydroxide is an antacid and laxative.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1508 (PDF p. 1817)
questions.quote: Simethicone is an antiflatulent used in the relief of pain caused by excessive gas in the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An older client is taking cimetidine. Which side effect should the home care nurse check for?
questions.rationale: Older adults are especially prone to cimetidine's CNS effects, the most frequent being confusion.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1509 (PDF p. 1818)
questions.quote: Older clients are especially susceptible to the central nervous system side effects of cimetidine. The most frequent of these is confusion.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which finding shows a client with gout is responding to colchicine?
questions.rationale: Colchicine blocks the white cell inflammatory response to urate crystals, decreasing joint pain, inflammation, and the number of attacks.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1513 (PDF p. 1823)
questions.quote: It interferes with the ability of the white blood cells to initiate and maintain an inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: What is the MOST common side effect of aluminum hydroxide antacid?
questions.rationale: Aluminum-based antacids cause constipation and can cause hypophosphatemia. They contain sodium, so they are used cautiously in hypertension and heart failure.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1515 (PDF p. 1825)
questions.quote: Because of the antacid’s aluminum base, aluminum hydroxide causes constipation as a side effect.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An older client has used casanthranol, a stimulant laxative, long-term. Which lab result is an adverse effect of this use?
questions.rationale: Long-term stimulant laxative use alters fluid and electrolyte transport and can cause hypokalemia. Normal potassium is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1518 (PDF p. 1827)
questions.quote: Hypokalemia can result from long-term use of casanthranol, which is a laxative.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: What is the MOST frequent side effect of cyclobenzaprine for muscle spasms?
questions.rationale: Cyclobenzaprine, a centrally acting muscle relaxant, most often causes drowsiness, dizziness, and dry mouth, so safety is a priority.
explanations: Correct: the most frequent side effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1519 (PDF p. 1829)
questions.quote: The most frequent side effects of cyclobenzaprine are drowsiness, dizziness, and dry mouth.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A man is prescribed metoprolol for hypertension. Which common side effect may affect his adherence?
questions.rationale: Impotence is a common side effect of beta blockers and may lead clients to stop the drug. Fatigue and weakness are also common.
explanations: Correct: a common reason for nonadherence.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1541 (PDF p. 1852)
questions.quote: A common side effect of beta-adrenergic blocking agents, such as metoprolol, is impotence.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client is on clozapine. Which laboratory value is the PRIORITY to monitor?
questions.rationale: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis and leukopenia. The WBC count is checked before treatment and closely during it, and the client is watched for sore throat and fever.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1545 (PDF p. 1857)
questions.quote: The white blood cell count should be assessed before initiating treatment and should be monitored closely during the use of this medication.
